A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same research despite substantial retitling and expansion. Their shared PTR/PPM framework, datasets, results, and proofs can be matched. Both complete documents, including appendices and graphical results, are readable.

before.justification: Section 7 and Appendix I report original experiments on six networks, including edge-density curves, runtime measurements, and privacy-budget sweeps.

after.justification: Section 8 and Appendix N report original density and runtime experiments, plus top-k eigenscore recovery results and empirical PTR success rates.

M1.justification: V2 Algorithm 1 adds a private spectral-gap test using truncated biased Laplace noise, a zero-distance branch for unfavorable inputs, and sensitivity-dependent test noise, thresholds, and beta selection. It returns a normalized private principal component, with subset selection handled separately. These substantially change v1's direct PTR procedure.

E1.justification: The same six network datasets are retained, but v2 adds an evaluated top-k eigenscore recovery task in Section 8.2 and Appendix N. Recovering the identities of high-centrality vertices introduces a different evaluation target from maximizing induced edge density. The expander discussion is theoretical, not an additional experimental dataset.

E2.justification: Corresponding density experiments retain PPM, the non-private rank-one method, and the density upper bound; Figure 1 retains the global-sensitivity Gaussian comparison. Calling PPM a baseline in v2 changes its positioning, not its participation. The new eigenscore experiments reuse existing methods.

E3.justification: V1 specifies delta = 1/m for PTR and 10^-12 for PPM; v2 specifies log(m)/m for both and adds the gap-test budget epsilon0 = 1, delta0 = 7 × 10^-7. The new eigenscore task uses Jaccard similarity against non-private subsets. These are substantive reported setting and evaluation changes.

E4.justification: The density-versus-privacy-budget analyses in v1 Appendix I are retained, with revised settings, in v2 Appendix N. V2 additionally checks empirical release success in Table 4 and extends privacy-budget sensitivity analysis to eigenscore recovery in Figures 7–8.

E5.justification: Density experiments retain 100 realizations and mean plus/minus one standard deviation. V2 separately reports 200 Monte Carlo trials for the new eigenscore comparison. This adds repeated-run information without establishing an increase in runs for the existing density experiments; no new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: V2 adds Jaccard-similarity results and PTR success rates of 96.9%–99.6% in Table 4. Density curves also change between v1 Figure 2 and v2 Figure 4 and in the appendix sweeps, under revised privacy settings. These are not same-setting performance gains. Table 1 sensitivity values and Table 3 timing values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 adds formal small-gap handling, the truncated biased Laplace mechanism, a new sensitivity analysis, and an all-graphs privacy theorem with expanded composition costs. It revises the success-probability and beta-selection results and adds expander-graph analysis in Appendix K. The non-private density bound is retained through relocation from v1 Proposition 3.1 to v2 Appendix M.

C1.justification: V1 presents two private DkS algorithms. V2 centers its contribution on a general, scalable private principal-component framework, presents DkS as a consequence, and explicitly treats PPM as a pre-existing baseline. The abstract and introduction also emphasize private screening of well-behaved graphs and the additional eigenscore application.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of gap-test and release-test failures, discusses increasing release probability or falling back to PPM, and relates favorable inputs to expander properties. It explains the revised privacy cost through three noisy quantities. These extend the retained interpretation of the privacy, utility, and runtime trade-off.

D1.justification: V2 adds an inverse-CDF sampling procedure for truncated Laplace noise in Appendix F and specifies its parameters. However, it omits v1's symmetrization, self-loop removal, and largest-connected-component preprocessing instructions and its promise to release code upon acceptance. Python and hardware descriptions remain unchanged; the omissions do not establish actual preprocessing or code-availability changes.

R1.justification: Beyond moving much of v1 Appendix A into Section 2, v2 adds substantial positioning around eigenvector centrality and its applications, expander graphs, and Xiao et al.'s truncated-noise mechanism. The contribution is repositioned as private principal-component estimation compared against PPM, rather than two proposed DkS approaches.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around principal-component estimation. Related work becomes a standalone section, DkS material moves into an Applications section and Appendix M, and the algorithm exposition is reorganized into three phases. This is substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: V2 adds a three-phase flow diagram, a main-text eigenscore figure, a success-rate table, and two appendix eigenscore-sweep figures. Algorithm 1 is substantially expanded, existing plot captions and legends are revised, and the density-sweep figures are consolidated. Table 2 also redisplays eigen-gap information previously available in Table 1.

improvement.justification: V2 broadens empirical validation and explains small-gap handling more clearly, but its revised release-probability guarantee has unresolved inconsistencies. Unlike v1's unit-sensitivity argument, Appendix J uses Laplace noise scaled by GS_phi without adjusting the tail exponent accordingly. Section 8.1 also specifies p = 1 - 1/log10(delta), which exceeds 1, despite Theorem 5 requiring p in (0,1]. These issues affect the claimed parameter-selection guarantee; together with removed preprocessing instructions, they prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
